lesson.title: The Hub: Ethernet's Loudest, Simplest Device
lesson.summary: A hub is a basic device that repeats every incoming signal out to all its other ports, with no awareness of addresses or destinations at all. Understanding why hubs were replaced by switches is one of the clearest lessons in why intelligence at the right layer matters.
lesson.body:
A hub is one of the simplest devices ever used to build an Ethernet network, and understanding it is mostly useful today as a contrast to everything a switch does better. A hub operates at the physical layer only: it has no concept of MAC addresses, frames, or destinations. Electrically, it just takes whatever signal arrives on one port, cleans it up and regenerates it, and repeats that same signal out every other port on the device. It is, in effect, a multiport repeater rather than a piece of networking intelligence.

Because a hub has no addressing logic, its forwarding behavior is trivial and total: flooding. Whatever comes in one port goes out all the other ports, unconditionally, whether the frame was meant for one specific device or not. The hub does not read the destination MAC address in the Ethernet frame at all; from the hub's point of view it is just handling raw electrical signals, and the job of figuring out whether a frame is relevant belongs entirely to the receiving network cards.

This flooding behavior has a serious consequence: every device attached to a hub shares the same transmission medium and the same total bandwidth, and only one device can transmit successfully at any given instant. If two devices happen to send at the same moment, their electrical signals collide and both transmissions are corrupted, which is exactly the problem that CSMA/CD, carrier sense multiple access with collision detection, exists to manage. All the ports on a hub belong to a single collision domain, a concept explored fully in a later chapter, and that domain only grows more congested as more devices are added.

Picture four PCs, A, B, C, and D, all plugged into the same hub, and suppose A sends a frame addressed to B. The hub has no idea the frame is meant only for B, so it repeats the signal out to B, C, and D simultaneously. B's network card reads the destination MAC address, recognizes its own address, and passes the frame up to the operating system. C and D's network cards also receive the identical electrical signal, check the destination MAC address, see that it does not match their own, and quietly discard it. The bandwidth cost of that frame, however, was paid on every link, not just the one that mattered.

This inefficiency, combined with the fact that every device on a hub can technically observe every other device's traffic, is exactly why hubs have been almost entirely displaced by switches in real networks. A switch performs the same physical job of connecting devices together but adds the addressing intelligence a hub lacks, forwarding frames only where they need to go rather than everywhere at once. Hubs still show up in networking courses because their dumb, brute force behavior is the cleanest possible baseline for understanding what a switch, and later a bridge, actually improves upon.
